title: EU countries to discuss AI rules as Trump calls safety warnings a ‘hoax’
content:
Government officials from across the European Union will gather in Brussels on Thursday to discuss how to set global rules to counter the threat from new AI models, according to two EU diplomats and a draft agenda seen by POLITICO.

The European Commission will give “updates on EU and international AI policy” and give a “technical briefing on recent AI incidents” during a gathering of the Artificial Intelligence Board, which comprises of representatives from every EU member country and regularly convenes to monitor progress on the bloc’s Artificial Intelligence Act.

This week’s gathering follows a series of calls to slow down AI development by top company leaders such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman. U.S. President Donald Trump immediately rebuffed the calls, calling the AI safety warnings a “hoax” and arguing that slowing down would give China the momentum in AI.

The European discussions on global cooperation will focus on work done at the G7, the G20 and the United Nations, one of the diplomats said.

Last Friday, the European Commission’s top tech official, Executive Vice President for Tech Sovereignty Henna Virkkunen, called for global AI rules and cooperation.

title: Carney puts exclamation point on Europe courtship with French archipelago visit
content:
PARIS — Mark Carney will wrap up a week spent shifting his country’s foreign policy toward Europe on Sunday with the first-ever visit by a Canadian prime minister to the obscure French territory of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, where he’ll meet President Emmanuel Macron.

The trip to the picturesque archipelago — a few kilometers off the south coast of the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador and home to fewer than 6,000 people — comes after Carney travels to Strasbourg for Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the European Union speech on Wednesday. The Canadian leader then journeys on to Liverpool to meet with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Carney and Macron will discuss cooperation on AI, energy, defense and critical minerals, according to a statement from the Canadian prime minister’s office. It is also Macron’s first trip there since taking office in 2017.

While Carney has for months sought to move Ottawa closer to Brussels and Paris as part of his middle powers alliance against the U.S. under President Donald Trump, the pivot has taken on renewed urgency amid the Canada-U.S. trade war, which has seen each side slap reciprocal tariffs on billions of dollars worth of goods.

title: Von der Leyen’s warring EU Parliament allies want her to pick a side. Can she appease them?
content:
STRASBOURG — The two biggest factions in the European Parliament want completely different things from Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech on Wednesday. If she can’t keep them both happy, the rift between these traditional centrist allies risks becoming a chasm as the far-right makes gains across the continent.

The center-right wants von der Leyen to double down on the simplification drive of the past two years while further toughening the bloc’s stance on migration in the wake of the Ceuta crisis. The center-left, meanwhile, wants a halt to what it calls the deregulation of EU green policies, and for von der Leyen to steer the center-right away from passing measures in the Parliament with far-right votes.

“We expect your address to send a clear political commitment that there will be no backtracking on the European Green Deal,” Iratxe García Pérez, president of the S&D group in the European Parliament, told von der Leyen in a letter, calling for “a change of focus away from deregulation.”

title: ‘SICK conspiracy going on against AI’: Trump bids to shut down regulation push
content:
President Donald Trump tried to shut down a burgeoning push for the United States to further regulate artificial intelligence on Monday morning, saying the U.S. has already done enough to prevent AI from catastrophic risks.

The post comes as technology leaders called for the industry to slow down the production of artificial intelligence over the weekend, sending tech stocks tumbling on Monday.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.

He added, “there is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”

title: ‘Horror in the sky’: Ukraine races for a solution to Russian jet-powered drones
content:
KYIV — Russia is upgrading its attack drones by powering them with fast turbojet engines, making them much more difficult to intercept and forcing Ukraine to develop technology to knock them down.

The shift is adding to the strain on a country already accustomed to nights spent under air-raid alerts: faster drones give air-defense crews less time to respond, can outpace the defenses that helped counter earlier Shaheds and threaten homes, transport and critical infrastructure across Ukraine.

“Together with dozens of Ukrainian companies, we are already looking for cheap and mass-produced solutions, in particular for intercepting jet-powered drones. Some interceptors are already undergoing combat testing,” Ukrainian Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara said last week at a meeting of Ukraine’s allies.

“We cannot simply wait while Russia refines its repertoire of killings. Right now, we need to focus as much attention as possible on securing the skies, finding ways to protect people, and scaling up our response to Russian drones,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last Friday.

title: Von der Leyen to skip Carney speech in EU Parliament
content:
STRASBOURG — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will not attend Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s address to the European Parliament on Thursday. 

Carney will speak to lawmakers on Thursday at 11.30 a.m. as he seeks closer ties with the EU amid deteriorating relations with Washington. He is expected to set out his wishlist for Brussels ahead of a Canada-EU summit in October. The address comes a day after he will attend von der Leyen’s annual State of the Union speech.

During Carney’s speech, the Commission will instead be represented by Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič — one of von der Leyen’s most trusted lieutenants — the executive’s chief spokesperson Paula Pinho confirmed.

The Commission president won’t be in Strasbourg on Thursday as she has to return to Brussels due to “prior commitments,” Pinho said. One of those prior commitments is a press conference on the child online safety initiative.
snippet: STRASBOURG — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will not attend Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s address to the European Parliament on Thursday.
creator: Max Griera

title: EU to limit access to social media before age of 15
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Commission will propose new rules to restrict minors’ access to social media and video-sharing platforms before the age of 15, according to preparatory documents seen by POLITICO and a person familiar with the matter.

The EU executive on Thursday will unveil a new EU KIDS Act setting out age restrictions, along with new rules requiring covered products, such as social media and AI companions, to be safe by design. The proposal aims to create a tiered system for accessing social media under parental supervision before age 15, the documents said.

The age restrictions are a major step by the European Commission and its President Ursula von der Leyen to better safeguard minors’ on social media platforms, amid a fierce backlash from health experts, politicians and parents against the effects of platforms like TikTok, Instagram and others on the mental health of minors.

It comes after months of intense pressure from government leaders, including France’s Emmanuel Macron, to put the issue at the top of the political agenda. Austria, Denmark, France, Greece and Spain are all pushing ahead with national laws to restrict kids’ access to social media.

title: The ideas shaping von der Leyen’s pitch to Carney
content:
From defense to critical raw materials, a new wave of EU-Canada agreements is on the horizon.

By MAX GRIERA, CAMILLE GIJS, GABRIEL GAVIN and
GERARDO FORTUNA in Brussels

Illustration by Natália Delgado/POLITICO

The EU is looking to pull Canada closer into its economic and security orbit as Donald Trump’s trade war forces Ottawa to seek allies beyond the U.S.

The offer under discussion spans critical minerals, digital trade, education, skilled workers and Arctic security. With Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney due to address the European Parliament this week and an EU-Canada summit set for October in Montreal, EU officials are weighing what Ursula von der Leyen can concretely offer in her State of the Union speech on Wednesday.

The aim is to deepen cooperation wherever it benefits both sides — and give Carney a way to show Canadians that Ottawa has powerful friends beyond Washington, 15 officials, politicians and diplomats told POLITICO.

The most ambitious proposals would bring Canada closer to the EU’s single market, expanding its existing trade ties with the bloc and moving it toward the level of integration enjoyed by nations such as Switzerland and Norway.
snippet:
From defense to critical raw materials, a new wave of EU-Canada agreements is on the horizon.

By MAX GRIERA, CAMILLE GIJS, GABRIEL GAVIN and GERARDO FORTUNA in Brussels

title: How to write a State of the Union speech
content:
Big promises, special guests and social media influencers have become a routine part of the EU’s most high-profile address.

By GABRIEL GAVIN
in Brussels

Illustration by Arnau Busquets Guàrdia/POLITICO

For the past six months, officials across Brussels have been feeding ideas, demands and policy pledges into Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech. Its contents, however, will remain a closely guarded secret until the European Commission president takes the podium on Wednesday.

The speech is the product of a sprawling process involving Commission departments, national officials, experts, lobbyists and interest groups. Yet the final decisions — what makes the cut, what is discarded and what becomes the central message — are made by a tiny circle around the president.

“There was a process where everybody would ask for something,” said Margaritis Schinas, a former Commission vice-president who helped prepare previous addresses. “But there was also a process where the president and the cabinet and ourselves were very clear on the few things to harvest that would make an impact.”

Big promises, special guests and social media influencers have become a routine part of the EU’s most high-profile address.

title: How did von der Leyen’s ‘independence moment’ hold up over 12 months?
content:
Ursula von der Leyen used her set piece speech last year to declare Europe’s “independence moment.” Twelve months later, the European Commission president’s record shows the EU’s independence still very much depends on its national capitals.

One year after her last State of the Union address, von der Leyen has delivered most clearly where the Commission could act largely on its own: writing laws and funding initiatives on core topics like tech, trade and social policy.

She struggled most where success required member countries to agree, surrender more control to Brussels or build genuinely new European capabilities — particularly on defense.

“The issue of defense plays a completely different role in Europe than it did just two years ago,” said Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, the liberal chair of the European Parliament’s security and defense committee, pointing to a series of “very valuable programs” launched over the past year.

But, she added, “all efforts are reaching their limits, because national self-interest continues to play a major role.”

That tension runs through POLITICO’s assessment of the promises in von der Leyen’s last State of the Union address.

title: ‘I don’t have any’: Trump brushes aside concerns over AI’s existential risks
content:
President Donald Trump downplayed concerns about the catastrophic risks of artificial intelligence raised this week by some AI researchers, saying late Thursday he was focused instead on the U.S. losing its edge in the tech arms race.

Asked whether he has concerns about existential risks posed by AI, the president said, “No, I don’t have any.

“I have concerns that if we don’t win AI, we’re going to be put in a very bad position,” Trump told reporters late Thursday as he left Dallas. “We are leading China right now by a pretty good period.”

Trump was wading into a debate over AI’s catastrophic risks ignited by a viral social media post from a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher. The post cautioned that the leading AI companies have been “gambling with our lives” and that some researchers working on the technology “believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

The post and the discourse it stirred up — along with recent alarming incidents where AI agents have gone rogue to launch hacking attacks — have prompted fresh calls from bipartisan lawmakers to rein in the fast-evolving technology.
snippet: President Donald Trump downplayed concerns about the catastrophic risks of artificial intelligence raised this week by some AI researchers, saying late Thursday he was focused instead on the U.S.
creator: Casey He

title: Escaping the AI safety nightmare: What can governments do?
content:
A dramatic resignation from AI company Anthropic this week where a researcher accused it and OpenAI of “gambling with our lives,” threw fuel onto the fire around AI safety.

As governments from California to the U.K. scramble for a political response to the issue of whether AI can be made safe, three experts told POLITICO that to make real progress, laboratories, governments and international bodies must first get on the same page about testing.

The steady flow of revelations that AI labs failed to contain models they were testing, allowing them out into the world where they lied, hacked and coordinated with each other, has heightened urgency to address core questions of how governments or other bodies can or should guarantee that AI is being developed and deployed safely.

Lawmakers, campaign groups and developers alike are calling for new laws and international treaties on AI. “It’s a wake-up call to the United States Congress, to parliaments all over the world, that we’ve got to do something immediately to stop the uncontrolled growth of AI,” U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders told BBC’s Newsnight program Thursday.
snippet: A dramatic resignation from AI company Anthropic this week where a researcher accused it and OpenAI of “gambling with our lives,” threw fuel onto the fire around AI safety.
creator: Frank Hersey

title: ‘Abuse of power’: Von der Leyen rapped after backing space mega deal
content:
BRUSSELS — A senior EU lawmaker has slammed Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s open endorsement of a space deal that awaits competition scrutiny as an “abuse of power”.

In a rare intervention on Thursday, von der Leyen told a space summit in Paris that she viewed a planned €6.5 billion joint venture between the bloc’s top satellite players as exactly the type of industrial champion that the bloc needs to lead in the space economy of tomorrow.

Her remarks drew a stinging rebuke from liberal MEP Stéphanie Yon-Courtin, who anchored the European Parliament’s last annual competition report.

“Endorsing a merger at a conference covered by the media, without any substantive review, is an abuse of power and misconduct,” the French MEP wrote on X.

Von der Leyen was referring to Project Bromo, a joint venture between satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales to compete, at least in part, with the Starlink satellite-internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which recently went public in the U.S. and is valued around $2 trillion.

“These are the types of industrial champions we need if Europe is to lead in the space economy of tomorrow,” von der Leyen said.
snippet: BRUSSELS — A senior EU lawmaker has slammed Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s open endorsement of a space deal that awaits competition scrutiny as an “abuse of power”.
creator: Francesca Micheletti

title: Iran-backed Houthis seize Red Sea port, putting another key trade route at risk
content:
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels seized the Red Sea port of Mokha and captured the nearby Perim island on Friday, tightening their grip around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait while the U.S.-Iran war chokes another of the world’s critical shipping routes at Hormuz.

The swift advance marks the Houthis’ biggest territorial expansion in years. According to reports from the Associated Press, fighters swept south along Yemen’s western coast as Saudi-backed government forces withdrew, prompting Saudi airstrikes on Mokha airport.

That surge puts the Houthis in a strong position around Bab al-Mandeb, the narrow southern gateway to the Red Sea and Suez Canal through which roughly 10 to 12 percent of global trade passes.

At its narrowest, the strait is only about 30 kilometers wide. Yemen’s internationally recognized President Rashad al-Alimi warned Thursday it “must not be allowed to become another Strait of Hormuz.”

The Iranian-supported rebel advance raises the prospect of simultaneous disruption at two of global trade’s most vital chokepoints, potentially compounding shipping delays, supply shortages and inflationary pressure worldwide.

title: EU Parliament ready to take tougher line on China, says lead MEP
content:
BRUSSELS — A cross-party consensus is growing in the European Parliament on the need for the EU to take a harder line on China, senior MEP Pascal Canfin told POLITICO.

Canfin, the European Parliament’s point person, or rapporteur, on the trade relationship with China, was scathing in his assessment of the threat posed by Beijing’s surging exports.

“The whole purpose of Chinese policy is to be the leader of the new global order based on their own power, their own values and the dictatorship of the Communist Party,” the French liberal said in an interview.

Brussels and Beijing are locked in negotiations over ways to rebalance the bloc’s €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with China. A surge in Chinese exports has put pressure on domestic producers, stoking fears that the continent is deindustrializing amid high-profile factory closures across the automotive and chemical sectors. 

EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič is set to visit Beijing in October as part of the talks. He has said that the bloc stands ready to act if progress is not made by that date.
snippet: BRUSSELS — A cross-party consensus is growing in the European Parliament on the need for the EU to take a harder line on China, senior MEP Pascal Canfin told POLITICO.
creator: Carlo Martuscelli, Jordyn Dahl

title: Keep calm and regulate on: Inside the EU’s response to AI extinction warnings
content:
BRUSSELS — A viral social media post warning that top American AI developers are “gambling with our lives” has been met this week in Brussels with business as usual — and a splash of Schadenfreude.

The European Union’s corridors of power were one of the few places over the past 48 hours not overtaken by a frenzy after an Anthropic employee announced he was quitting, with a stark warning that the people building AI “earnestly believe” that the artificial intelligence models they’re building “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Multiple EU policymakers responded to questions about such a threat by noting that Brussels already has a law for that: the bloc’s Artificial Intelligence Act.

Others noted that the dire AI extinction warning could actually be a chance for the bloc’s highest officials to regain control over the AI narrative. Since the groundbreaking 2022 release of ChatGPT, the EU was repeatedly mocked by tech enthusiasts for regulating a still-emerging technology.
snippet: BRUSSELS — A viral social media post warning that top American AI developers are “gambling with our lives” has been met this week in Brussels with business as usual — and a splash of Schadenfreude.
creator: Pieter Haeck

title: Bad actors in China and Russia are already weaponizing Anthropic’s AI
content:
Killer drones. Mass surveillance. Bioweapons.

Artificial intelligence threats that might have seemed like science fiction nightmares just a year ago are much closer to reality today, according to AI powerhouse Anthropic. And some may already be here.

In a lengthy new report out Thursday, Anthropic said that criminal hacking gangs, Chinese security bureaus, Russia-linked spies and Yemen-based arms manufacturers, among others, have exploited a web of fraudulent accounts and online services to access some of the company’s advanced AI assistants, known as Claude.

And they’re using those tools to attempt attacks or design weapons that previously lay beyond their capabilities.

In the last eight months alone, Anthropic said, people in countries where Claude should be restricted circumvented those controls to automate cyberattacks, try designing advanced military hardware, spread propaganda at scale and mount broad digital surveillance campaigns. Though Claude models are broadly available commercially, Anthropic tries to restrict access in major U.S. adversaries, including Russia, China and Iran.
snippet: Killer drones. Mass surveillance. Bioweapons.
creator: John Sakellariadis

title: Macron’s space summit showed Europe isn’t ready for takeoff without the US
content:
PARIS — The international space summit hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday and Thursday was meant to show that Europe is getting serious about investing in its space sector.

But the two-day gathering under the glass dome of Paris’ Grand Palais ended up demonstrating that Europeans are not spending enough to cut reliance on the U.S. to access space — at least not yet.

On the sidelines of the summit, space companies from around the world announced billions in new partnerships and investments, but the big get-together fell short of the public funding announcements needed to access space without U.S. help.

Things had already started to look bad a few days before the summit when American space companies such as SpaceX decided to ditch the event after White House pressure, accusing France of “anti-competitive practices” and disregarding the perspectives of U.S. industry. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also skipped the event, despite it being co-chaired by France and Germany. 

French officials downplayed the importance of the U.S. absence, stressing that the summit would provide Europe with an opportunity to step up its game on space.
snippet: PARIS — The international space summit hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday and Thursday was meant to show that Europe is getting serious about investing in its space sector.

title: Putin’s bot army is targeting German and French elections, Sweden warns
content:
STOCKHOLM — Russia poses a threat to upcoming elections in Europe’s biggest democracies and social media platforms must “step up” the fight against Moscow’s networks of bots, Sweden’s disinformation defense chief has warned. 

In an interview with POLITICO, Magnus Hjort, director general of the Swedish Psychological Defence Agency, said elections were an “opportunity” for Vladimir Putin’s information war machine to try to polarize and divide European societies.

The Kremlin’s key objective is to make voters doubt whether their politicians should keep sending money and weapons to Kyiv by peddling fake stories about Ukrainian corruption and other abuses, he added.

Hjort and his team do not believe Moscow is targeting Sunday’s general election in Sweden — in part because the country is largely united behind the policy of supporting Ukraine.

Instead, he said, Russia is aiming at more powerful countries with elections on the horizon — including German state votes and the French presidential campaign — where far-right parties seen as more sympathetic to Moscow are poised to make gains.

title: Von der Leyen backs space mega-deal despite looming EU antitrust probe
content:
PARIS — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has publicly endorsed a proposed space venture between Airbus, Leonardo and Thales — a rare intervention by a top EU official in an ongoing competition matter — as the satellite-makers seek Brussels’ approval for the deal.

EU officials generally refrain from commenting on open antitrust proceedings. The Commission received a rap on the knuckles in 2015 from the European Ombudsman after former competition chief Joaquín Almunia made public comments on an ongoing investigation into a banking cartel. 

Von der Leyen’s high-profile backing comes as the three satellite-makers hold informal talks with the Commission’s competition directorate on the €6.5 billion deal, which raises complex antitrust issues and could require divestments to win approval. They have yet to submit a formal notification for a merger review.

She is also a prime mover behind an overhaul of the EU’s merger guidelines, which in addition to traditional competition concerns would allow greater latitude for mergers that create so-called European champions.

title: Bernie Sanders to host AI briefing for US senators
content:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) will host a private briefing for senators next week with top artificial intelligence researchers, according to a letter to colleagues obtained by POLITICO.

The meeting, slated for 4 p.m. on Sept. 16, comes as concerns grow on both sides of the aisle about safety warnings from top AI labs and researchers about the technology’s growing capabilities.

“Congress needs SERIOUS discussions about this issue,” Sanders wrote. “That is why I will be convening a private briefing with some of the leading experts in the world to discuss this recent incident and the extraordinary dangers that AI poses for humanity.”

Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the “godfather of AI,” is expected to brief the lawmakers alongside MIT professor and co-founder of the Future of Life Institute Max Tegmark and Ajeya Cotra, an independent investigator who helped probe OpenAI agents’ recent autonomous attack on the tech platform Hugging Face.
snippet: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) will host a private briefing for senators next week with top artificial intelligence researchers, according to a letter to colleagues obtained by POLITICO.
creator: Owen Dahlkamp

title: US Democrats prepare to put AI under a new microscope
content:
House Democrats are laying the groundwork for a select committee on artificial intelligence should they retake control of the House in November, 11 people familiar with the planning told POLITICO.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been briefed on the effort and expressed openness to the idea, four of those people said. All 11 people were granted anonymity to discuss details of private deliberations.

The discussions offer an early glimpse of how Democrats could use their new gavels and expanded oversight powers to scrutinize the tech industry.

House select committees are usually created by a full House vote and last only for the two years of the Congress that created them. Gaining buy-in from members who sit on committees that currently oversee AI policy may prove difficult.

The Energy and Commerce; Judiciary; and Science, Space and Technology committees all oversee slices of the AI policy portfolio. Its chairs and members will likely be reluctant to give up any jurisdiction of the issue, especially at a pivotal stage in shaping the rules governing the technology, two of the people said.
snippet: House Democrats are laying the groundwork for a select committee on artificial intelligence should they retake control of the House in November, 11 people familiar with the planning told POLITICO.
creator: Jacob Wendler, Owen Dahlkamp

title: How Emmanuel Macron brought France’s AI darling to the world stage
content:
Mistral has forged unrivaled ties with the French presidency. Now, Emmanuel Macron is departing.

By OCÉANE HERRERO
in Paris

Illustrations by Björn Griesbach for POLITICO

It’s not every AI company that can count the French president as its top salesman.

On June 11, 2025, the founder of French AI company Mistral took to the stage alongside Jensen Huang, the powerful CEO of chip giant Nvidia, to announce a partnership between the two companies. As President Emmanuel Macron joined them, the Taiwanese-American executive turned to Mistral’s young CEO Arthur Mensch and said something just audible to the Parisian audience of techies and public officials: “Your president worked really hard for you.”

The Nvidia boss was referring to the deal his company had just sealed with Mistral to roll out AI infrastructure across Europe. “I told the president that Arthur and Mistral needed support from France’s biggest companies. Mr. President said to me: ‘Which ones? Let me call them!’” Huang said.
snippet:
Mistral has forged unrivaled ties with the French presidency. Now, Emmanuel Macron is departing.

By OCÉANE HERREROin Paris

title: US lawmakers urge Congress to act after AI researcher’s dire warning
content:
Lawmakers in Washington from both parties are escalating pleas for legislative action after an artificial intelligence researcher claimed late Tuesday that unchecked AI models could feasibly destroy the world by the decade’s end — and AI developers know it.

While it’s not the first time experts have warned of the existential threats posed by an unregulated industry that is rapidly advancing, it comes at a moment of heightened awareness on Capitol Hill about the need to reach consensus on AI safety legislation before it’s too late.

“The call is coming from inside the house,” Rep. Lori Trahan of Massachusetts, a House Democrat seeking to lead her party on AI policy, posted on X Wednesday. “Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway.”

She was responding to social media posts from former Anthropic AI researcher Jason Coxon, whose warnings were first reported in the Wall Street Journal.

title: EU seeks to transform procurement into €600B driver of industry
content:
BRUSSELS — The EU wants to transform public procurement into a powerful tool of industrial policy by channeling hundreds of billions of euros spent on infrastructure, schools, energy or health toward European businesses.

In its Public Procurement Act unveiled on Wednesday, Ursula von der Leyen’s Commission is following up on recommendations by economic reform guru Mario Draghi to give a lift to struggling European industry while shielding the bloc from external risks in an increasingly uncertain world.

The sums involved are huge. Public procurement represents up to 15 percent of the EU’s GDP — or around €2.5 trillion a year. Of that, some €600 billion is governed by EU rules, Executive Vice President Stéphane Séjourné told reporters.

“This is public money, which must also serve our collective goals,” the French commissioner said. “It’s the equivalent of a yearly recovery plan and about four to five times the EU budget in terms of spending.”

title: The Draghi plan at 2: Competitiveness crusade runs into Europe’s old politics
content:
BRUSSELS — Two years after Mario Draghi warned that Europe faced an “existential” threat from economic decline, his plan to make the continent competitive again has become the EU’s official agenda — but implementation lags behind rhetoric.

The Commission has proposed a series of Draghi-inspired measures, from an industrial policy overhaul to new funding for competitiveness and defense. Yet grand ambition has come up against the realities of the EU legislative machine, and many proposals remain stuck in negotiations as national governments continue to defend their spending priorities and policymaking turf.

A year ago, Draghi didn’t sound too happy with how quickly his plan was being implemented. Since then, his frustration with the lack of progress has become increasingly visible. The former Italian prime minister recently co-founded the Rhine Group with Stripe chief Patrick Collison, bringing together business leaders, economists and former policymakers to push Europe from diagnosis to action.

title: 7 things Ursula von der Leyen will say in her State of the Union speech
content:
Here’s what the European Commission president will announce in her biggest address of the year.

By SEBASTIAN STARCEVIC
in Brussels

Photo-Illustration by Natália Delgado/POLITICO

Ursula von der Leyen has pegged her political legacy to making Europe more independent in a dangerous world. On Wednesday, the European Commission president will have to explain how that’s going — and what’s next.

As the EU deals with wars, wildfires and Donald Trump, von der Leyen will use her sixth State of the Union speech to lay out her agenda: climate-proofing Europe; catching up with China and the U.S. on artificial intelligence; turbocharging the bloc’s defense industry; and reforming its migration rules.

The speech will be revised and rewritten right up to the point she delivers it. But based on conversations with more than a dozen European officials, granted anonymity to discuss the president’s priorities and talking points, here’s what POLITICO’s newsroom has heard she will say.

title: OpenAI backs binding UK AI legislation
content:
LONDON — OpenAI’s top European lobbyist is calling for the U.K. to introduce binding rules on AI developers in light of the technology’s rapidly advancing capabilities, and the risks that come with them.

Tom Duff Gordon, the company’s head of policy in EMEA, told POLITICO in an interview that the “U.K. should act now to set up a stronger set of safety rules.”

“OpenAI is in a position to support legislation in the U.K. to establish durable, mandatory, capability-based requirements for frontier AI that would build on the set of voluntary commitments that we currently have,” said Duff Gordon.

He said Andy Burnham’s government should “take advantage of this political window which is clearly opening up” to pursue legislation.

The Labour government is facing mounting pressure from lawmakers to address the risks of AI after leading companies disclosed a spate of safety incidents in recent months. That pressure intensified last week after a researcher at AI company Anthropic resigned and accused Anthropic and OpenAI, where he’d previously worked, of “gambling with our lives.”

title: EU tech chief backs global AI rules in wake of extinction warning
content:
DUBLIN — The European Union is calling for global artificial intelligence rules, its top tech official said Friday, after a viral warning from a former Anthropic engineer said AI could end humanity.

“It’s very important we continue now the international cooperation here, because I see that global rules are really needed,” the European Commission’s Executive Vice President Henna Virkkunen said on the sidelines of a conference in Dublin on online safety for children.

The EU has a law requiring companies including Anthropic and OpenAI to assess and mitigate the risk of losing control of an AI model, but “that is not the case globally,” Virkkunen said.

The bloc has consistently called for global cooperation on the risks stemming from the technology. At the G7 in France in June, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said “Europe and the U.S. should work together on AI,” citing “complementary strengths, shared security interests, and a common responsibility to lead.”

title: California’s Newsom signs online kid safety laws, including rules backed by Sam Altman
content:
SACRAMENTO, California — Gov. Gavin Newsom on Thursday greenlit sweeping new child safety rules for social media and AI chatbots, including a law backed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, amid mounting political pressure to regulate tech giants.

Newsom’s decision to sign the bills comes at a pivotal moment for Silicon Valley. State and national lawmakers are calling for stricter AI regulations after current and former researchers for Anthropic and OpenAI warned this week that the technology, if left unchecked, poses existential risks to humanity. Meta, Google, Snap and TikTok are also facing hundreds of child safety lawsuits, including a blockbuster case Meta settled last month by agreeing to pay states up to $18 billion.

But Newsom, a likely 2028 presidential candidate, called the settlement a “drop in the bucket” — and he argued that the federal government should expand on California’s online safety rules.

title: Everyone wants a line in the State of the Union speech
content:
BRUSSELS — Walk through the EU Quarter of Brussels and you’ll see posters plastered on walls and telephone poles asking European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to give animal welfare a starring role in her State of the Union address.

“Your words matter,” the posters read. “Include animals in your speech.”

As von der Leyen prepares for her big speech on Sept. 16, everyone from the largest lobby groups to cash-strapped NGOs — and even apparently guerrilla campaigners (none of the big animal welfare groups POLITICO spoke to took responsibility for the posters) — are making their pitch for a few precious seconds of the Commission president’s time.

Some are taking the conventional approach. Last month, almost 200 industry associations and national groups signed a letter addressed to von der Leyen demanding she use her speech to commission an expansive, Mario Draghi-style report into the bloc’s appetite for fossil fuels.

title: EU reveals its first discovery of cyber vulnerabilities using OpenAI frontier models
content:
BRUSSELS — After months of urgent pleas, the European Union finally got access in July to some of the most powerful AI models coming out of Silicon Valley. Now, the EU’s cybersecurity teams say they’ve put those U.S.-built tools to good use to spot weaknesses in the bloc’s own digital systems.

Cyber agency ENISA and technical defense team CERT-EU used frontier AI models to find four flaws in source code used for a European Union project, ENISA spokesperson Laura Heuvinck confirmed Thursday to POLITICO. 

The EU cyber authorities used an advanced model from ChatGPT-maker OpenAI to conduct a “security analysis” of the code, Heuvinck said. That work led to the discovery of the four weaknesses — known in the cyber world as vulnerabilities — including one rated as “high” risk and could be used to hijack accounts. The flaws have since been fixed.

The use of the latest artificial intelligence tools to identify the flaws had not been reported previously. Their discovery will be seen by the agency as tangible proof to justify their long-running attempts to always get early access to the most advanced AI frontier models.

title: EU watchdog probes von der Leyen’s AI envoy pick
content:
The EU ombudsman has opened an inquiry into the European Commission’s appointment of Siemens chairman Jim Hagemann Snabe as special envoy for industrial AI.

A group of NGOs complained to the EU watchdog about the decision, warning that Snabe’s ongoing role at Siemens “may compromise the envoy’s independence and impartiality.”

That same group — including Transparency International, Corporate Europe Observatory, LobbyControl and the Good Lobby — wrote to the Commission on June 10 with their concerns about the move, but said they received no response.

Snabe will serve in the unpaid role until the end of March 2027 and is expected to produce a report on issues including AI infrastructure, frontier AI technologies and industrial AI adoption. 

But the appointment came under fire because of Siemens’ recent role in lobbying to loosen the AI rules now shaping Europe’s industrial strategy. 

Siemens was one of the main proponents of exempting products covered by the EU’s machinery rules from the bloc’s flagship AI law — a tweak EU legislators agreed to in the summer and which is now part of the law.
